usage: 어디가 asks the spot, the doctor's opener
examples: 저 오늘 좀 아파요.
I'm a little sick today.
좀 softens it to 'a bit' — telling someone you feel off
배가 아파서 학교에 못 갔어요.
My stomach hurt so I couldn't go to school.
아파서 = the reason; pairs naturally with 못 갔어요
많이 아프시면 병원에 꼭 가 보세요.
If it hurts a lot, please be sure to see a doctor.
아프시면 adds 시 to respect the listener's body
nuance: 아프다 covers both a specific body part hurting (배가 아파요 = my stomach hurts) and the whole-body state of being unwell/sick. The crucial point for English speakers: it is a descriptive adjective, not an action verb, so you describe yourself as 아파요, never 아파해요 — that -해요 ending belongs to verbs like 좋아해요. To say WHAT hurts, the hurting part takes the subject particle 이/가, not 을/를: 머리가 아파요, never 머리를 아파요, because nothing is doing an action to the head; the head simply is in a hurting state. The stem 아프- is ㅡ-irregular: before the -아/어 ending the bare ㅡ drops and, because the remaining vowel ㅏ is bright, 아 is chosen, giving 아 + 아 → 아파요 (not 아프어요). Compare 아프다 with 슬프다 (sad): both are emotional/physical states ending in -프다 and both drop ㅡ the same way (슬퍼요), so once you master 아파요 the pattern transfers. Note the polite/respectful form for an elder is 편찮으세요, a separate honorific word you would use instead of 아프세요 for grandparents.

examples: 손이 더러워요. 씻고 오세요.
Your hands are dirty. Go wash them.
everyday hygiene reminder; note 더러워요 not 더럽어요
바닥이 더러워서 청소했어요.
The floor was dirty so I cleaned it.
더러워서 gives the cause, leading to the action 청소했어요
이 컵은 더러우니까 다른 거 주세요.
This cup is dirty, so please give me another one.
더러우니까 = 'since it's dirty', justifying a request
nuance: 더럽다 is the everyday word for physically dirty/filthy — a smudged hand, a grimy floor, an unwashed cup. Its clean opposite is 깨끗하다 (clean), and the near-synonym to keep apart is 지저분하다: 더럽다 stresses actual filth/grime (sticky, stained, germy), while 지저분하다 leans toward 'messy/cluttered/untidy' — a desk piled with papers is 지저분해요 even if nothing is grimy, whereas a toilet is 더러워요. 더럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: before a vowel ending the final ㅂ of the stem changes to 우, so 더럽- + -어요 → 더러워요, and the noun-modifying form is 더러운 N (더러운 옷), never 더럽은. Beyond the literal sense, Koreans also use 더럽다 figuratively for a 'foul/rotten' temper or situation — 성격이 더럽다 means someone has a nasty disposition — so context decides whether it is hygiene or attitude. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like a regular stem and producing 더럽어요/더럽은; the ㅂ MUST soften to 우. Compare with 춥다 (cold) and 무겁다 (heavy), which conjugate identically (추워요, 무거워요), so the whole ㅂ-irregular family follows one rule.

usage: 있다-type modifier is 재미있는, not 재미있은
examples: 이 게임 진짜 재미있어요!
This game is really fun!
casual reaction; 진짜 = 'for real' in speech
한국어 공부가 재미있어요.
Studying Korean is fun.
the thing judged fun takes 이/가, not 을/를
어제 본 영화가 재미있었어요.
The movie I saw yesterday was fun.
past tense 재미있었어요 from 재미있- + -었어요
nuance: 재미있다 is literally 재미 (fun, enjoyment) + 있다 (to exist) — 'fun exists [in it]' — which is exactly why it conjugates like 있다 and gives 재미있어요, and why the noun-modifying form is the 있다-style 재미있는 N (재미있는 영화), never 재미있은. It spans both English 'fun' and 'interesting': a party, a game, or a class can all be 재미있어요, so let context choose the English. The near-synonym to separate is 재미있다 vs 흥미롭다: 재미있다 is the warm, everyday 'enjoyable/entertaining' you say about a movie or a friend, while 흥미롭다 is a cooler, more bookish 'intriguing/of interest' you might use for a research finding or a phenomenon — calling a thrilling roller coaster 흥미로워요 sounds oddly academic. Its direct opposite is the single word 재미없다 (재미 + 없다, 'fun does not exist') = boring; do not say 안 재미있다 as your default negative — 재미없어요 is the natural 'it's boring', and 안 재미있어요 reads more like 'it's not [particularly] fun'. The big English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation: because the headword ends in 있다, learners over-apply -하다 or vowel rules and produce 재미있다요 or 재미있아요; the only correct polite form is 재미있어요, with past 재미있었어요.

usage: the safe, respectful way to ask an adult's age
examples: 나이가 어떻게 되세요?
May I ask how old you are?
polite question to an adult or stranger
우리는 나이가 같아서 말 편하게 해요.
We're the same age, so we speak casually.
same age (나이가 같다) often licenses 반말
나이보다 어려 보이세요.
You look younger than your age.
나이보다 = 'than [your] age', a common compliment
nuance: 나이 is the native Korean word for a person's age, and it sits at the center of Korean social life because age sets who speaks formally to whom. Register is everything: to an adult, an elder, or a stranger you ask 나이가 어떻게 되세요? (or even more deferential 연세가 어떻게 되세요?, using the honorific 연세 for grandparents), while the blunt 몇 살이에요? is reserved for children or close friends — asking your boss 몇 살이에요? sounds rude. The near-synonym pair is 나이 vs 연세: same meaning, but 연세 (年歲, Sino-Korean) is the respectful 'years' you grant to someone older, so you raise the register by swapping the word, not by adding an ending. Crucially, age is measured with 많다/적다, not size words: 나이가 많아요 = 'is old', 나이가 적어요 = 'is young' — never 나이가 커요, a direct-translation trap from English 'big'. When you state an actual number, age takes NATIVE numbers + the counter 살: 스무 살 (20), 서른 살 (30) — saying 이십 살 with Sino-Korean numbers is a classic beginner error. One more pitfall: the verb is 되세요 (from 되다, 'to become/amount to'), so 어떻게 되세요? literally asks 'how does it come to be?' — treat the whole phrase as a fixed polite formula rather than translating it word by word.
